grade.first_issue: The first decisive defect is the claim that the union P of all prime divisors of the terms is finite. The asserted implication that infinitely many such primes would force some a_{n+1} to contain a prime p>a_n+M is false. For example, if a_1=2, then a_n=2n, so P contains every prime and is infinite. Thus the central finiteness argument is false and Rule E caps the score at 3.
grade.summary: The submission establishes some useful preliminary facts, including bounded gaps and that every sequence term lies in the globally admissible set C. However, its central route to periodicity depends on the demonstrably false assertion that only finitely many primes occur among all terms. A fundamentally different structural finiteness argument is required. The final passage from eventual to pure periodicity is also unsupported.
strengths: Correctly translates the gcd conditions into intersections of prime supports.
Correctly observes that multiples of the radical of a_1 are always admissible, yielding the uniform bound a_{n+1}-a_n≤M.
Correctly defines the global admissible set C and proves that every a_n belongs to it.

errors.description: The proof that P is finite is invalid, and the claim itself is false. In the valid sequence beginning with a_1=2, the terms are 2,4,6,8,…, whose prime divisors comprise all primes. In particular, new primes can enter gradually with p comparable to a_n/2, so no prime exceeding a_n+M is forced.
The inequality claim that M<p≤a_n+M implies (a_n+M)/p<2 for sufficiently large a_n is false; for fixed p>M, the quotient instead grows with a_n.

Even an eventual equality C_n=C would directly give only eventual periodicity. The assertion that a_1 is the first element of C is false in general (for example, with a_1=6 the sequence continues 8,10,12,… while 2,4∈C), and determinism does not by itself propagate an eventual translation law backward. One instead needs to prove that the sequence enumerates C∩[a_1,∞) from the outset.
